Caricatures and the wars they started

Project 36 · a satire, with a real table · index

Label. Everything below takes political cartoons at their word, which no one should. Cartoonists drew rulers as effeminate or as walking moustaches for reasons of politics, not anatomy; the point of this page is that if you sort wars by the cartoon, the cartoon predicts nothing, and that is the joke. Dates are real. The categories are not.

1. The feminised caricature

To draw a ruler as womanish was the oldest way to say he was unfit. Aristophanes did it to Cleisthenes. Gillray drew Napoleon as “Little Boney”, a tantrum in a big hat. Henri III of France was drawn surrounded by his mignons in lace and earrings, and the pamphlets of the League called him a hermaphrodite. James I was called “Queen James” in London taverns. Louis XIV wore red heels, a full wig and ribbons and was, by the standards of 1680, the most masculine object in Europe; by the standards of a 1920s textbook illustration he became a peacock. Xerxes was pierced and gilded by Hollywood in 2006. And Dwight Eisenhower, who had commanded the largest invasion in history, was drawn by Herblock for eight years as a grinning, passive man in golf clothes who let other people run things — not womanish exactly, but the cartoon of a man who does not fight.

2. The over-masculine caricature

The other cartoon is the moustache with a man behind it. Kaiser Wilhelm II, spiked helmet, upturned whiskers, one arm withered from birth and the uniforms chosen to hide it. Mussolini, jaw first, shirtless at the harvest. Theodore Roosevelt, teeth and spectacles and a big stick. Charles XII of Sweden, who never married, slept in his boots and was drawn as a sword with a face. And the modern one, shirtless on a horse. These men commissioned their own caricatures; the cartoonists merely traced.

3. The experiment

Take one war per ruler, the one most associated with them, and time it. Where the ruler did not start the war, say so and time it anyway, since the cartoon does not care about causation either.

4. Findings, stated with a straight face

  • The feminised caricatures fought longer wars. Mean length of the feminised rows, counting Eisenhower’s six months and James’s zero: about 7 years. Mean of the over-masculine rows: about 7 years too, but only because Charles XII drags the whole column up single-handed, which is on brand. Remove him and the moustaches average under two years. The peacocks average twelve.
  • The man drawn as least likely to fight fought the most. Louis XIV, the ribbons and heels, spent thirty-two of his fifty-four adult years at war. The man drawn as a spiked helmet managed one war and lost his throne in it.
  • The only ruler on the table who started no war at all was the one the taverns called Queen. James I kept England out of the Thirty Years’ War against the wishes of Parliament, his son and most of his cartoonists. The cartoon was, in that one respect, accurate and approving without meaning to be.
  • Eisenhower, the golfer, is the only entry whose number measures how fast a war was ended. Six months from inauguration to armistice. He then declined to bomb Dien Bien Phu, which is the shortest war on the table because it did not happen. The advisers he sent to Saigon are in project 37, and that column is longer.

5. When a caricature of a woman wanted to get home

The table has a control group of one. Helen of Sparta is the most caricatured woman in the Western canon — a face, a launch count, a woman written entirely from the outside — and in the Odyssey she is home in Sparta, mixing a drug into the wine so no one at dinner cries. Getting her there took:

LegLengthCompared to
The war fought to bring her home10 yearslonger than the Kaiser, Mussolini, Roosevelt and Xerxes combined
Menelaus’s wandering home with her, by way of Egypt (Odyssey book 4)8 yearslonger than the First World War, twice
Total, from abduction to dinner~18 yearsbeaten only by Charles XII and Edward II, neither of whom got home either

Odysseus, for comparison, took ten years to get home from the same war and is the one with the epic named after him. Penelope, who never left, waited twenty. The finding is that the longest campaign on the page was a woman’s commute, and the second-longest was another woman’s wait, and neither was drawn with a moustache.

6. What the satire is actually about

The cartoon’s claim was that a man who dresses that way will not fight, and a man who dresses this way will. The table says the cartoon is a costume, and the war is decided by borders, treasuries and alliances that do not read cartoons. This page belongs next to project 35 only as its footnote.
